title: New York Army Band and lessons with Sonny Igoe
summary: He plays concert and stage band at Governor's Island and studies the Bellson/Breines book with Sonny Igoe on a government lesson plan.

story.theme_name: Drafted: musicians in the military and the war years
story.community_name: Drafted: service bands, USO shows and the war years

blocks.x: No — yes, this was a concert band. We played parades up and down Fifth Avenue, you know, the whole bit. But then there’d be the symphonic band, I mean the concert band, and I was good a tympani because that’s what I played in high school, because of my ear, and I could tune and play the tympani and all that. So I wound up playing — so in other words all the guys in the percussion are saying they’re supposed to alternate playing with what they call the stage band then, you know, the New York Army Stage Band, which are now called the Jazz Ensemble or whatever. And nobody could, none of those guys could swing. I mean they just couldn’t do it. So as soon as I hit — but I couldn’t read very well. I mean I could read music but I couldn’t read swing music the way I should have been, I could read concert band music, but I didn’t quite have it. But getting back to one of your former interviewees I guess was Sonny Igoe. Now I had met Sonny down at Nick’s. In fact I’ve even got photos of Sonny giving me — sending drum sticks home and a photo of him and my father and then a photo of me with him. I actually look like him because I wore horn-rimmed glasses, and we look the same. I’ve got it upstairs someplace. So he sent me drumsticks home. But he was teaching upstairs over Henry Adler’s studio. Now the band director that came in to the New York Army Band replaced a marching band director and the new director was named Mr. Shettle S-H-E-T-T-L-E. And he had come from the Seventh Army Symphony, which was the only symphony in the Army and I mean these guys were just so ragged. I mean he wanted a symphony orchestra. He did not want a marching band. But he was now transferred to the New York Army Band. And he’d be holding the tubas down and, you know, like shhhh, you know, “you’re playing too loud.” I mean it was a tremendous marching band, but he wanted

music not balls to the walls bluster. So he decided to get everybody a thing where the government paid for lessons. Well you could pick your own teacher. And I went up to Henry and I sought Sonny downstairs, and I said, “man, I’d really like to study with you.” And I said, “I’ve been on the road with the Salt City Six” and this and that, “and I’m in the New York Army Band.” And he wasn’t being facetious I don’t think, but he knew me and — we’re not friends yet, but when I said I’d been on the road with the Salt City Six and he had been with Billy Maxted’s band and he did a thing called the “Big Crash from China” which is beautiful. He said, “well maybe you don’t need me.” I said, “no man, don’t get me wrong man, I need you, I really do need you.” So he took me on and the government paid him his checks, eight weeks at a time, three dollars a lesson. And after the first lesson he put the thing down and he said, “I can see you’re a swinger.” But he got me onto this Bellson/Breines B-R-E-I-N-E-S. Bellson/Breines book. It was a breakthrough. I mean he would sit with me at the pad, the drums would be over there, and we’d play it and he said, “now this is the way that these are supposed to” — and we’d hum it and play it together. So all of a sudden that was what I needed to be able to read big band music. I can’t read eighth notes like I’m going to read them in a concert band. I’ve got to read them in swing figures. And it wasn’t — you didn’t have Thad Jones-Mel Lewis charts in those days, or you know like even Basie charts you know And then we’d do the first half hour that way, then the second half hour we’d go to the set, he’d put the headphones on and have me start reading like Broadway stuff. Because he was the drummer with “The Gary Moore Show,” and had been on several shows. He was a staff musician. I’ve got to tell you — I talked to him a month or two before he died. I used to call him on a regular basis. I really liked Sonny. But that was the breakthrough with all of that. Then he did come over to Eddie Condon’s one time when I was playing with my own band The Metropolitan Bopera House — we’ll get to that. And it was what I needed, I really needed. I’d take off in the morning and get on the Staten Island Ferry, because now we were over — well Governor’s Island was transferred to the Coast Guard and we were transferred over to Staten Island. And I played the final ceremony. So that’s why when I go down to Governor’s Island I’m one of the last people from the Army, because I was 20, I go there, I was there a couple of weeks ago, I look in that band room and all I see is ghosts because those guys are like, a lot of those lifers were 40 years old and it kind of hurts. And then they opened it up for me last year, the old barracks, and I said, “can we go up in the attic,” I said, “there’s a lot of things that were a little un-military-like that took place up there. And I looked on the floor and there weren’t any seeds.
